Family Health

STI symptoms in men: what to notice and when to get tested

Updated: October 12, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Sexually transmitted infections can cause discharge, burning, sores or other symptoms, but many cause none. Symptoms overlap with nonsexual conditions, and appearance cannot identify an infection reliably. Testing and appropriate care protect your health and your partners without blame or assumptions about when an infection began.

Symptoms are a reason to seek care, not a diagnosis

Arrange a sexual-health or medical assessment for penile discharge, burning when urinating, genital or mouth sores, new growths, rectal pain, discharge or bleeding, or a partner’s diagnosis. Tell the clinician about oral, anal and vaginal contact so testing includes the relevant sites. Do not wait for visible symptoms after a known exposure.

Seek emergency care immediately for sudden severe testicle pain, testicle pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or pain lasting over an hour or continuing at rest: torsion can threaten the testicle. New testicular swelling needs urgent assessment too. Do not assume pain is an STI or wait for a routine test to exclude an emergency.

Chlamydia

Chlamydia is a bacterial infection transmitted through vaginal, anal or oral sex. It often causes no symptoms; when symptoms occur they may take weeks. Men may notice burning during urination, penile discharge or, less commonly, testicular pain or swelling. Rectal infection can cause pain, discharge or bleeding, or be silent.

Urine or site-appropriate swab tests help diagnose it. Prescribed antibiotics can cure the infection, but do not reverse damage already present and do not prevent reinfection. Complete treatment, follow the clinic’s advice about partners and when sex can resume, and arrange repeat testing, commonly around three months after treatment.

Gonorrhea

Gonorrhea is another bacterial infection that can affect the urethra, rectum or throat. Symptoms can include burning urination, white, yellow or green penile discharge, and sometimes painful or swollen testicles. Rectal infection can cause itching, soreness, discharge, bleeding or painful bowel movements; infections at any site may be unrecognized.

Discharge colour does not distinguish gonorrhea from other causes. Testing may require urine plus throat or rectal swabs according to exposure. Treatment must account for antibiotic resistance. Rare spread to blood or joints can be serious: fever with a painful swollen joint or rash needs urgent assessment. Follow prescribed treatment, partner care and repeat-testing advice; persistent symptoms need reassessment.

Hepatitis A is caused by HAV, not HIV

Hepatitis A is a liver infection caused by the hepatitis A virus, HAV. It spreads when tiny amounts of infected stool reach the mouth, including through contaminated food or water and some sexual practices, particularly oral–anal contact. Contaminated raw shellfish can be a food-related source. It is not limited to sexual transmission.

Symptoms can include tiredness, fever, poor appetite, nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, dark urine, pale stools and yellow eyes or skin. Most people recover with supportive care, but serious liver illness can occur. Vaccination and careful handwashing with soap and water are important; barriers alone cannot guarantee prevention. Seek prompt advice after an exposure because vaccine, sometimes with immune globulin, may help within two weeks.

Hepatitis B and silent liver infection

Hepatitis B is caused by HBV and spreads through infected blood, semen and certain other body fluids, including during sex. Infection may be acute or become chronic. Many people feel well while liver damage develops, so lack of genital symptoms or a flu-like illness cannot establish whether infection is present.

Possible symptoms include poor appetite, fatigue, fever, aches or joint pain, nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, dark urine, pale stools and jaundice. Blood testing and follow-up assess infection and liver health. Acute and chronic care differ; selected chronic infections need antiviral treatment and ongoing monitoring. Vaccination prevents infection. New jaundice needs medical assessment, and recent exposure warrants prompt advice about prevention.

Herpes: HSV is different from HPV

Genital herpes can be caused by HSV-1 or HSV-2. HSV-1 often affects the mouth, but either type can cause genital infection; oral sex can transmit oral HSV to the genitals. Many people have mild or unnoticed symptoms and can pass the virus without visible sores. Tingling, itching or burning may precede painful blisters or ulcers around the genitals, anus or mouth.

A first recognized outbreak can include fever, body aches, tender groin glands and feeling unwell; recurrent outbreaks can be milder. Timing or appearance cannot reliably identify who transmitted it. A fresh sore can be swabbed, while blood tests have limits and are not routine screening for everyone. Antiviral treatment can shorten or suppress outbreaks but does not eradicate HSV. Avoid sexual contact during sores or warning symptoms, and discuss ongoing prevention with the clinician.

HPV: warts and cancer risk are different issues

Human papillomavirus is a large group of viruses spread through intimate skin contact, including vaginal, anal and oral sex. Most infections cause no symptoms and many clear without harm. Some types cause genital warts: flat or raised bumps, sometimes in clusters resembling cauliflower. Persistent high-risk types can cause penile, anal or throat cancers; wart-causing types are different from cancer-causing types.

New genital, mouth or throat lumps, sores or persistent changes need assessment rather than a diagnosis from a photograph. There is no routine test that establishes a man’s overall “HPV status” or screens the mouth and throat for HPV. Clinicians can assess visible lesions and relevant cancer concerns. Treating warts does not guarantee that the virus is gone, and a late diagnosis does not prove a recent transmission.

HPV vaccines: products and ages matter

Gardasil 9 targets nine HPV types: 6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52 and 58. It includes wart-associated and cancer-associated types. Cervarix targets types 16 and 18; it does not provide the same 6/11 wart coverage. Vaccines prevent new infections and related disease, not an existing infection or current warts. Available products and national schedules differ.

In the United States, CDC recommends routine HPV vaccination at 11–12 years, starting as early as 9, and catch-up through 26 if not adequately vaccinated. Some adults aged 27–45 may benefit after an individual discussion; it is not routinely recommended for everyone in this range. FDA licensing through age 45 does not mean approval above 45. Ask about your local schedule, earlier doses and immune status rather than choosing a course yourself.

Syphilis can change stages without being cured

Syphilis is bacterial and spreads through contact with an infectious sore during oral, vaginal or anal sex. Primary infection may cause one or more sores on the penis, anus or mouth, often firm and painless but not always, with nearby swollen glands. A sore can heal without treatment while infection remains. Secondary infection may cause a rash, including palms or soles, fever, sore throat, headache, fatigue and swollen glands.

Latent syphilis has no visible symptoms but remains in the body. Untreated infection can later damage the heart, blood vessels and other organs. Brain, nerve, eye or ear involvement can occur at any stage, not only late disease. New vision or hearing changes, eye pain or neurological symptoms need urgent assessment. Appropriate antibiotics can cure infection but may not undo damage; follow-up blood tests and partner care remain necessary.

Testing and HIV prevention after an exposure

No single urine or blood test checks every STI. The clinician chooses tests and sampling sites from symptoms, exposures, vaccination and local recommendations. Blood tests may assess HIV, syphilis or hepatitis; urine and swabs assess other infections. A test taken too early can be negative despite infection, so ask about the window period and repeat testing. HIV self-test positives need confirmatory testing.

For a recent possible HIV exposure, seek assessment immediately for post-exposure prophylaxis, or PEP: it must start within 72 hours, and sooner is better. Do not wait for symptoms or a test window. Discuss PrEP for ongoing HIV risk; it does not prevent other STIs. Prompt HIV diagnosis and treatment improve health; maintaining an undetectable viral load prevents sexual transmission. Testing frequency depends on individual risk and local guidance, not symptoms alone.

Reducing risk without assuming complete protection

Use condoms correctly for vaginal or anal sex and appropriate barriers for oral contact. They reduce risk but cannot cover every area that transmits herpes, HPV or syphilis. Avoid contact with sores and, for herpes, prodromal tingling or burning. Avoid fecal–oral contact and wash hands after toileting or handling materials exposed to stool and before food preparation.

Reducing partners or a mutually monogamous relationship with an appropriately tested uninfected partner can reduce exposure. Vaccination can prevent hepatitis A, hepatitis B and selected HPV types, but not every STI. Avoiding sexual contact prevents sexual exposure, not all nonsexual transmission of hepatitis. Discuss prevention without stigma: having no symptoms, one partner or a previous negative result is not a lifetime guarantee.

Treatment, partners and follow-up

If an infection is diagnosed, follow its specific treatment and partner-notification plan. A clinic can help partners obtain assessment and treatment where appropriate, including when they have no symptoms. Do not share antibiotics, use leftovers or assume every partner needs identical medicine. Ask exactly how long to avoid sex, whether symptoms must resolve and which follow-up tests are needed.

Seek review for persistent or returning symptoms. New jaundice, severe illness or fever with joint swelling needs urgent medical advice; new eye, hearing or neurological changes also need urgent assessment. If a partner is pregnant, their maternity team should know promptly about relevant exposure or diagnosis. Keep vaccination and testing records, but never let an app reminder delay time-sensitive exposure care or emergency assessment.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Current CDC guidance emphasizes asymptomatic infection, exposure-based testing and partner care. A symptom list or a single test cannot establish every STI status.

HPV vaccine product coverage, national recommendations and regulatory licensed ages are distinct. Vaccination prevents new infection rather than treating existing HPV.

HIV PEP requires immediate assessment within 72 hours; test window periods do not justify delaying it. Sudden or persistent testicular pain can be a separate surgical emergency.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help track vaccination dates, testing appointments, medicines and questions for a confidential sexual-health consultation. It cannot diagnose an STI from symptoms or determine a safe testing window. Follow the clinic’s plan and seek immediate exposure or emergency care when needed.

When to seek help

Get emergency care for sudden severe testicular pain, pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or pain lasting over an hour or at rest. Seek immediate PEP assessment after a possible recent HIV exposure; do not wait for symptoms. New jaundice, eye or hearing changes, neurological symptoms or fever with a swollen joint needs urgent assessment. Do not self-treat with leftover or shared antibiotics.

Evidence notes updated: October 12, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Many STIs are silent, and similar symptoms can have different causes; testing must match exposure sites.
  • HAV, HBV, HIV, HSV and HPV are distinct viruses with different prevention and treatment.
  • Vaccines and barriers reduce specific risks; they do not provide complete protection against every infection.
  • Possible recent HIV exposure needs immediate PEP assessment; emergency testicle pain must not wait for STI testing.

Frequently asked questions

What symptoms can hepatitis B cause in men?

Often none. Possible symptoms include fatigue, poor appetite, fever, aches, nausea or vomiting, abdominal discomfort, dark urine, pale stools and jaundice. Blood testing is needed; feeling well does not exclude chronic liver infection.

What are common HPV symptoms in men?

Most infections cause no symptoms. Some types cause genital warts, including flat or raised bumps or clusters. HPV is different from herpes: painful blisters and tingling are not a reliable HPV diagnosis. New genital, mouth or throat changes need assessment.

Can vaccines prevent STIs?

Vaccines can prevent hepatitis A, hepatitis B and selected HPV types, but not every STI. They are not treatment for an existing infection. Ask about local recommendations and your vaccination history; HPV products and eligible ages differ.

Do condoms prevent all STIs?

Correct use reduces risk but does not eliminate it, particularly for infections spread from uncovered skin or sores. Oral barriers can also reduce exposure. Vaccination, appropriate testing and partner care remain important.

Can I have an STI with no symptoms?

Yes, and it may still spread or cause complications. Ask about testing after a partner’s diagnosis or relevant exposure. The right tests and repeat timing depend on the infection, contact sites and test window periods.

How quickly should I seek care after possible HIV exposure?

Immediately. PEP must start within 72 hours and works best when started sooner. Do not wait for symptoms or a test result. A clinician determines whether it is appropriate and arranges follow-up; PrEP may suit ongoing risk.

Do sores healing or treatment mean I cannot get infected again?

No. A syphilis sore can heal while infection remains. Treatment of a bacterial STI does not prevent reinfection; HSV can recur and HPV may persist. Follow the specific partner, sexual-contact and repeat-testing plan.

When is testicular pain an emergency?

Get emergency care immediately for sudden severe pain, pain with nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain, or pain lasting over an hour or continuing at rest. Torsion needs rapid treatment. Do not wait for STI testing; new swelling or worrying discomfort also needs urgent assessment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
